interactions.label: Why can kidneys and corneas be transplanted from a recently deceased donor, but

params.question: Why can kidneys and corneas be transplanted from a recently deceased donor, but brain function cannot be restored?

answers.text: Kidney and corneal cells do not require oxygen, so they remain viable indefinitely after death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Kidney and corneal cells do require oxygen. They survive longer after circulatory arrest because their metabolic demand is lower than that of neurons, not because they are oxygen-independent.

answers.text: Brain neurons suffer irreversible damage within 4–6 minutes of circulatory arrest, whereas kidney tubule cells can survive up to 2 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Neurons have the highest oxygen demand and are the first cells to undergo irreversible damage after somatic death. Kidney tubule cells tolerate ischaemia for up to 2 hours, providing a transplant window that the brain does not have.

answers.text: Transplantation technology has been developed for kidneys but not yet for brain tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The limitation is biological, not technological. Brain neurons die irreversibly within minutes of circulatory arrest, long before any surgical procedure could restore them.

answers.text: The brain is the last organ to undergo cellular death, making retrieval logistically impossible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The brain is actually the first organ to undergo irreversible cellular death because of its very high metabolic rate. It is the most vulnerable tissue after circulatory arrest.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the cellular death timeline: neurons die within 4–6 minutes, cardiac muscle within 20–30 minutes, and kidney tubule cells survive up to 2 hours. This staggered sequence explains why certain organs can still be transplanted from a recently deceased donor.

Well done. The staggered timeline of cellular death — neurons first (4–6 min), cardiac muscle (20–30 min), kidneys (up to 2 hr) — is why organ harvesting is possible even though brain function can never be restored.

interactions.label: Under Indian law, accidental deaths are classified as natural deaths and do not

params.question: Under Indian law, accidental deaths are classified as natural deaths and do not require reporting to the police.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Accidental deaths — including falls, road accidents, and drowning — are classified as unnatural under Indian law. Even though no one intended the harm, they must be reported to the police for investigation.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Despite the absence of intent to harm, accidental deaths are classified as unnatural under Indian law. Falls, road accidents, and drowning must all be reported to the police for investigation.

params.question: A 28-year-old patient on ventilatory support after a severe head injury is suspected to be brain dead, and the family consents to organ donation. Under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA), who must certify brain death?

answers.text: The treating physician alone, provided they hold a postgraduate qualification in neurology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A single physician, regardless of qualification, cannot certify brain death for organ transplantation under THOTA. The Act requires a multi-member board to guard against errors in this irreversible determination.

answers.text: A board of four doctors: the hospital head or nominee, the treating physician, a neurologist or neurosurgeon, and a government-appointed doctor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. THOTA mandates this specific four-member board for brain death certification in organ transplantation cases, ensuring that the determination is rigorous and multi-disciplinary.

answers.text: Any two registered medical practitioners, with at least one being a specialist in intensive care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: THOTA specifies a four-member board with defined roles, not merely any two practitioners. Each member serves a specific oversight function in the certification process.

answers.text: A magistrate along with two government-appointed doctors, as brain death is a medicolegal determination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Brain death certification under THOTA is a medical determination, not a judicial one. The four-member board is composed entirely of physicians, though one must be government-appointed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Under THOTA, brain death for organ transplantation must be certified by a board of four: (1) the hospital head or nominee, (2) the treating physician, (3) a neurologist or neurosurgeon, and (4) a government-appointed doctor.

Well done. The four-member board requirement under THOTA ensures that brain death certification for organ transplantation involves multiple independent clinical assessments, safeguarding against misdiagnosis.

interactions.label: What is the biochemical mechanism responsible for rigor mortis?

params.question: What is the biochemical mechanism responsible for rigor mortis?

answers.text: Accumulation of lactic acid causes sustained involuntary muscle contraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although lactic acid accumulates after death due to anaerobic metabolism, it is not the direct cause of rigor mortis. The stiffening results from permanent cross-bridge formation when ATP is depleted.

answers.text: Depletion of ATP locks actin-myosin cross-bridges in a contracted state, preventing muscle relaxation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ATP is required for the detachment of myosin heads from actin filaments. When ATP is depleted after death, the cross-bridges remain locked, producing the characteristic stiffness of rigor mortis.

answers.text: Bacterial enzymes from early putrefaction cause degradation and stiffening of muscle proteins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial action causes the opposite effect — it breaks down muscle tissue and causes softening during putrefaction. Rigor mortis is a chemical process that occurs before bacterial decomposition begins.

answers.text: Coagulation of blood within intramuscular capillaries restricts muscle movement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Post-mortem blood pooling (lividity) is a separate phenomenon from rigor mortis. Rigor mortis is caused by changes within the muscle cells themselves — specifically ATP depletion — not by vascular changes.

overallFeedback.feedback: Rigor mortis is caused by ATP depletion after death. Normally, ATP allows myosin to detach from actin after contraction. Without ATP, the actin-myosin cross-bridges remain permanently locked, producing progressive muscle stiffness.

Well done. Rigor mortis results from ATP depletion: without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin, locking muscles in a rigid state. It begins in small muscles (face, jaw) within 1–2 hours and resolves at 24–36 hours.

interactions.label: A body is recovered from a shallow, waterlogged grave after several months. The

params.question: A body is recovered from a shallow, waterlogged grave after several months. The subcutaneous fat has transformed into a firm, waxy substance that has preserved the body's shape and wound tracks. Which post-mortem change has occurred?

answers.text: Mummification, caused by dry, warm, well-ventilated conditions drawing out tissue moisture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mummification requires dry, warm, well-ventilated conditions — the opposite of a waterlogged grave. It produces a shrunken, leathery, dark body rather than a waxy transformation of fat.

answers.text: Adipocere formation, caused by saponification of body fat in warm, moist, oxygen-poor conditions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Adipocere forms when body fat undergoes saponification in warm, moist, anaerobic conditions — exactly what a waterlogged grave provides. It can preserve body shape and wound tracks for years.

answers.text: Advanced putrefaction with waxy bacterial deposits on the body surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Putrefaction causes tissue liquefaction and eventual skeletonisation, not a firm, waxy transformation. The preservation of body shape and wound tracks described here is characteristic of adipocere, not putrefaction.

answers.text: Maceration, caused by prolonged immersion in a sterile fluid environment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Maceration is a bacteria-free process occurring in a sterile fluid environment, most notably affecting a foetus that has died in utero. It does not produce a waxy transformation of subcutaneous fat.

overallFeedback.feedback: The waxy transformation of body fat in moist, oxygen-poor conditions is adipocere, formed by saponification. Unlike putrefaction (which destroys tissue) or mummification (which requires dry conditions), adipocere preserves body shape and wounds.

Well done. Adipocere is forensically valuable because it can preserve wound tracks and identity features for years. Each late post-mortem change depends on the environment — moist and anaerobic for adipocere, dry and ventilated for mummification.

interactions.label: In a suspected firearm suicide, the weapon is found tightly gripped in the decea

params.question: In a suspected firearm suicide, the weapon is found tightly gripped in the deceased's hand and cannot be easily pried away. What is the forensic significance of this finding?

answers.text: It indicates rigor mortis has fully developed, suggesting death occurred at least 6–12 hours ago

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rigor mortis develops gradually over hours and affects all muscles progressively. Cadaveric spasm, by contrast, occurs instantaneously at the moment of death in the muscles that were in intense use — and it cannot be reproduced after death.

answers.text: It represents cadaveric spasm, which strongly supports that the deceased was holding the weapon at the moment of death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cadaveric spasm is an instantaneous stiffening of muscles in intense use at the moment of death. Unlike rigor mortis, it cannot be reproduced after death, making it strong evidence that the deceased was gripping the weapon when they died.

answers.text: It is evidence that someone placed the weapon in the hand after death and forced the fingers closed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cadaveric spasm cannot be faked or reproduced by placing an object in a dead person's hand. Its presence actually argues against staging, since it occurs only at the instant of death in actively contracting muscles.

answers.text: It is inconclusive and requires fingerprint analysis on the weapon before any inference can be drawn

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While fingerprint analysis may supplement the investigation, cadaveric spasm alone is a recognised forensic sign with clear evidentiary value. Its presence strongly indicates the deceased was actively gripping the weapon at death.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cadaveric spasm is an instantaneous stiffening at the moment of death, distinct from the gradual onset of rigor mortis. In firearm cases, a spasm-gripped weapon strongly supports that the deceased was holding it when they died.

Well done. Cadaveric spasm is forensically important because it cannot be reproduced after death. In firearm and drowning cases, it provides direct evidence of what the deceased was doing at the instant of death.
